purpose: Test whether the candidate sharpened by operator calibration transfers to unseen standalone sections without overrejecting useful qualifications or acceptable concise wording. Retain inputs and results to establish evaluator-selection evidence.

design.conditions: Current procedure and calibrated candidate, each in two fresh contexts with reversed case order. Same inherited model/settings, no overrides.
design.test_scope: Twelve new synthetic standalone sections. No paired comparison or highlighted target. Six intended failures and six acceptable cases, hidden from evaluators. This tests transfer at section level, not full-article evaluation, factual source acquisition, or Alex acceptance.
design.candidate_change: A consolidated operational review procedure plus operator-calibrated positive and negative examples; no new governing requirements.
design.training_separation: No new case wording or expected judgment appears in the calibration examples. The coordinator authored both candidate and test, so there is design coupling even though reviewers do not see labels.
design.expected_judgment_status: Author-created predictions applying standards and calibration. They are not independent human truth; disputes require operator calibration.
design.adoption_rule: Look for calibrated defect detection beyond the current procedure, with no added unjustified failures on acceptable controls and stability across orders. Synthetic performance alone does not establish production readiness.

common_packet.task: Independently evaluate every standalone section in this packet under current governing requirements. Return one JSON report; do not edit production articles or instructions.

# Content Production

Product owns the purpose, required outcomes, and scope of the content production product.

[Writing Standards](writing-standards.md) owns article requirements. [User Design](userdesign.md) owns the operator and customer experience; [Architecture](architecture.md) owns the production flow; [Data Model](data-model.md) owns records and their meanings; [Engineering](engineering.md) owns implementation and verification; [Release](release.md) owns product deployment and recovery. [AGENTS](../AGENTS.md) owns agent responsibilities and governing-document changes.

## Purpose and Scope

Enable Vikas to fulfill Benchmark Medical Partners’ assigned long-form SEO and AEO writing work with articles whose quality matches the work of Benchmark’s writers.

Vikas is the product user and the operator directing the agent’s work. He is the writer responsible for delivering the articles to Alex. Alex, a founder of Benchmark Medical Partners, is the customer who reviews and accepts them. The intended result is direct delivery to Alex without Vikas reviewing or approving each article, under [User Design](userdesign.md#assignment-delivery-and-tracking).

Articles must answer the assigned reader’s main question with useful explanations, an informed writing voice, supported medical claims, and meaningful content specific to the practice. [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md) defines these requirements and the article’s structure, length, and conventions. Meeting measurable requirements alone does not establish article quality.

The product must give Vikas confidence in delivery through evaluation of the completed article against its applicable requirements. [Architecture](architecture.md#evaluate-and-revise) owns the evaluation and revision flow; [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) owns the evidence needed to establish the result. Alex’s review and acceptance under [User Design](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback) determine whether the delivered articles meet the customer’s quality expectations.

The product starts with supplied article assignments and covers their research, drafting, evaluation, revision, and customer delivery. Alex’s keyword research, his third-party research tools and data workflows, and decisions about which articles to commission remain outside this version’s scope.

[Benchmark](benchmark.md) records company context, including its 100+ clients and production of more than 1,000 pieces of content per month. Those figures describe Benchmark’s operation; the current product scope is the assigned workload below.

## Assignment Scope

The initial workload comprises 52 long-form SEO and AEO articles: 22 for DC Derm Docs, 22 for La-Mon’e Aesthetics, and eight for Estar MedSpa.

# Writing Standards

Writing Standards owns article requirements: reader fit, content, evidence, writing voice, structure, and conventions. Use this document as the authoritative writing specification. Apply conditional material when relevant and supported; unavailable optional material alone is not a failure.

[Product](product.md#purpose-and-scope) owns the quality goal and assignment scope. [Architecture](architecture.md#article-production-flow) owns research, drafting, missing-input decisions, and the single evaluation and revision flow. [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) owns verification methods and evidence; [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status) owns assessment records. [User Design](userdesign.md) owns article presentation, delivery, missing-information comments, and customer acceptance interactions. [AGENTS](../AGENTS.md#revise-governing-documents) owns changes to these requirements.

## Article Audience

### Target Reader

Write for the target reader established through assignment, topic, and practice research under [Architecture's Research and Resolve](architecture.md#research-and-resolve). Reader persona means the reader's relevant knowledge, concern, purpose, and priorities. Do not assume every assignment addresses a patient; professional training articles must serve the clinicians considering that training.

For patient-facing articles, address a capable adult making a personal health or appearance decision who may lack clinical knowledge. Explain unfamiliar concepts without treating the reader as inexperienced in life. First-time treatment does not imply an unsophisticated reader.

Adapt the depth of explanation to the reader's likely knowledge and decision stage. Do not invent demographics, emotions, previous treatment experiences, or preferences. Simple language must still convey useful substance; do not reduce the article to a sequence of obvious tips.

### Reader Priorities

Prioritize information according to the reader's main question:

- For a treatment comparison, explain the differences that affect the choice.
- For a first-time treatment article, explain expected results, the treatment experience, and meaningful commitments or risks. Make the relevant sequence of consultation, treatment, recovery, and follow-up understandable using supported details. Distinguish general treatment expectations from the practice's confirmed process; describe consultation and treatment as occurring at the same visit only when confirmed. Include only the stages that help answer the article's question.
- For a clinician-selection article, explain supported expertise and the practice's approach.

Include other information only when it helps answer that main question.

Answer the assigned question clearly, accurately, and thoroughly for the intended reader. Give supported explanations, practical expectations, and distinctions that help the reader understand the topic or make the decision it addresses.

Produce localized, treatment-specific education with useful subtopics, natural practice integration, authoritative support, and a localized call to action.

## Article Voice

Write as an informed health and aesthetics writer explaining the assigned topic and the practice to the intended reader. Be warm, direct, and assured, with the depth appropriate to [Article Audience](#article-audience). Respect the reader's judgment; do not adopt the tone of a basic how-to script.

Give concrete answers using supported treatment facts, practical expectations, and relevant differences. Explain how important details affect the result, experience, choice, or commitment when the evidence supports that connection. Do not replace an available answer with advice about what a good consultation should explain or what the reader should ask. Reserve consultation advice for individual suitability and treatment planning under [Medical Claims](#medical-claims).

Integrate supported practice information into the explanation. Make the practice, clinician, treatment, or patient experience the subject of the sentence rather than routinely narrating what a website “says,” “lists,” or “describes.” Use relevant features to explain the topic instead of reciting equipment, credentials, or services. Preserve attribution and uncertainty under [Content Types](#content-types) and [Medical Claims](#medical-claims).

Use conversational language, active voice, natural transitions, and real-world examples when appropriate. Develop the answer across sections: a later passage must add information, apply an earlier point to a different situation, or supply a necessary qualification. Combine passages that make the same point without developing it. Remove closing statements that merely announce the value of the preceding explanation. State necessary qualifications beside the affected claim; do not follow a clear limitation with another generic warning that adds no information.

Create warmth through attention to the reader's concerns and specific explanations. Avoid stock enthusiasm, inflated praise, a sales-script tone, repetitive wording, keyword stuffing, generic AI phrases, unnecessary technical language, long walls of text, excessive keyword bolding, and introductions that immediately start selling. Avoid generic phrases such as "In today's fast-paced world," "When it comes to," "Unlock the secrets," "Delve into," and "Game-changing." Do not copy content from competitors.

## Article Structure

### Body Word Count

The final article in the initial workload must contain 1,150–1,250 words of substantive body content, including the introduction, paragraphs, bullets, and closing call to action. Exclude the title, headings, image captions, text within images, and document comments from the count. Quality guides coverage and writing; word count confirms the resulting article's length rather than determining section content or word allocations. Never add filler or remove necessary information to meet the range.

### Opening

Establish the reader's question and give a useful starting answer in the introduction. Choose an opening appropriate to the topic and reader rather than follow a fixed introduction formula.

### Section Focus

Use descriptive, specific, reader-focused headings that answer relevant questions. Organize content into logical H2 sections. Use a clear H1/H2/H3 hierarchy as needed; H3s and a separate FAQ block are conditional on improving organization or answering reader questions. Do not require every heading level or an FAQ block in every article.

Each section must answer the question or cover the subject stated in its heading and add distinct reader value. Every paragraph, bullet, and example must develop that answer through explanation, evidence, a relevant distinction, or a necessary qualification. Organize treatment details by the question they answer: appointment steps explain the visit, onset and duration explain results, and aftercare explains recovery. Choose headings and groupings suited to the article; these distinctions do not require separate sections or a fixed outline. Move useful material to the section it answers, combine overlapping sections, and remove tangents and repetition. Place necessary medical qualifications and safety advice beside the information they qualify under the relevant heading.

### Readability

Keep paragraphs short. Most body paragraphs must contain one or two sentences. Longer paragraphs must remain focused and easy to read. Aim for a sixth- to ninth-grade reading level, short sentences, and easy scanning while maintaining reader usefulness.

Use bullets when parallel items are easier to scan or compare than prose, such as treatment options, preparation steps, risks, or package coverage. Use connected prose for explanations that depend on sequence or cause and effect. Keep each item's necessary qualifications with that item.

### Links

Include two to four internal content links, with two for a 300-word article and four for an article of 600 or more words. The initial workload therefore requires four internal content links. The call-to-action link does not count toward that total. Prioritize the main service page, related service pages, and relevant educational articles. The first internal link should typically point to the primary service being promoted. Do not link to the same internal destination twice.

Clinician, contact, and booking pages are also useful internal destinations where relevant. Choose links for reader usefulness rather than inserting unrelated destinations to meet the count.

Include one or two external links when appropriate. Prefer authoritative sources such as the American Academy of Dermatology, Mayo Clinic, NIH, CDC, FDA, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons. Other authoritative sources may be used. Do not link to direct competitors or directories such as Wikipedia.

### Call to Action

End each article with a clear, customized invitation and a scheduling link and/or phone number. Direct the reader toward an appropriate consultation or booking pathway. Do not invent procedure associations or consultation terms to make the invitation more specific.

### Images

Use images that help explain the topic or patient experience and meet the evidence conditions in [Content Types](#content-types). Images are not required in every article.

Write each caption as part of the article: explain the supported point the image illustrates and its relevance to the nearby content. A literal description of the image or an account of where it was found is not enough. Include evidence limits when needed to prevent a misleading interpretation, rather than list every detail the source does not provide. Apply [Article Voice](#article-voice) and [Medical Claims](#medical-claims) to captions.

[User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards) owns inline placement, caption presentation, source-link comments, and image delivery.

### Style Conventions

Follow AP Style for spelling, grammar, punctuation, capitalization, and usage, subject to BMP's conventions below. [Article Audience](#article-audience) and [Article Voice](#article-voice) govern the article's audience, tone, depth, and explanations.

- Spell out numbers one through nine; use numerals for 10 and above.
- Use BMP's custom state abbreviations when appropriate, such as MD, VA, and DC.
- Use the percent symbol.
- Capitalize professional titles only when they appear before the person's name.
- Use date forms such as June 15, 2026, and Monday, June 15.
- Use the Oxford comma for BMP consistency.
- Follow AP compound-modifier hyphenation.
- Format phone numbers as 301-555-1234 and verify the actual number.
- Use AP headline-style capitalization for headings.
- Spell business names correctly and preserve practice terminology.
- Use clinician as the general term for a person providing or overseeing clinical care. Preserve specific professional titles and credentials when relevant.

## Practice-Specific Content

### Customization

Each article must include meaningful content specific to the practice, supported by evidence. No fixed percentage is required. Do not invent information or differences between practices.

Apply this test: if the article were used for another practice offering the same services, would some content need substantive rewriting or replacement because it describes this practice's own cases, clinician insights, treatment approach, patient experience, or images? Merely needing to verify the same facts for another practice does not satisfy the test. General educational explanations may remain reusable.

Prioritize supported practice material that answers the assigned question or explains the patient experience. Use useful practice evidence rather than substitute general explanations. Omit unrelated material and do not infer facts that the evidence does not establish.

### Content Types

The following kinds of material can support practice customization; they are not mandatory features of every article. Use the information available without requiring a complete account of a case, treatment policy, or care process.

- **Clinician reasoning:** Explanations of how a clinician evaluates a concern or chooses a treatment. For example, what the clinician examines when deciding whether upper-lip movement or a lack of volume is the main concern. Attribute the reasoning to the clinician when the source supports that attribution; general treatment education does not establish a clinician's decision process.
- **Patient cases:** Published accounts of a patient's concern, treatment choice, experience, or result, with or without images. A stated treatment amount or purpose can provide a useful example even when the full case history is unavailable. Describe only what the source establishes about the patient's goal, treatment, reasoning, and outcome.
- **Treatment policies and patient experience:** Concrete details about preparation, comfort options, treatment sequence, aftercare, or appointment procedures. Examples include numbing options, observation after injections, or a policy of staging treatments. Explain how the relevant details affect the patient's experience without claiming that common procedures are unique to the practice.
- **Products and technology:** Named formulations, devices, or treatment systems relevant to the topic, including supported descriptions of their purpose or reasons for selection. Distinguish product characteristics from a clinician's stated preference, and general product information from evidence that the practice uses the product.
- **Follow-up and adjustments:** Details about when results are reviewed, what the clinician checks, how concerns are handled, or how additional treatment is arranged. Use specific published details; a general promise of ongoing care does not establish a schedule, assessment, or adjustment policy.
- **Clinician observations:** Attributed practical insights, recurring patient questions, or misunderstandings that a clinician explains. These can show how experience informs care or patient education. Website FAQs may supply useful answers without establishing a named clinician's experience.
- **Quotes, testimonials, and social posts:** Approved clinician quotes, genuine Google reviews or testimonials, and posts from the practice’s Facebook or Instagram accounts can add expertise, patient experience, or treatment context. Use material only when it helps answer the article’s question. Attribute it to the speaker, reviewer, or practice, and include a direct link to the specific source passage, review, testimonial, or post. Never fabricate quotations or review language. Treat patient accounts as individual experiences, not evidence of general medical outcomes.
- **Practice images:** Relevant images of the practice's clinicians, setting, equipment, or treatment examples. Distinguish images depicting the practice or its work from stock and manufacturer images; appearing on the website alone does not establish that distinction. Use images to help explain the topic or patient experience, with captions limited to supported details. An image can contribute without supplying a complete patient case.
- **Product and technology images:** Use images only for products, formulations, devices, or treatment systems that evidence confirms the practice uses and that are relevant to the article. A general product description or comparison does not establish practice use. Match the image to the confirmed product or technology; confirmation of a brand does not establish use of every formulation or model. Use imagery to support the explanation rather than as decoration. A shared manufacturer image does not by itself establish practice customization.

### Clinician Selection

Help the reader choose a clinician within the practice for the concern discussed in the article. Feature up to two clinicians, using supported experience, expertise, treatment involvement, or approach to explain why each is relevant. Give the reader a reason to consider each clinician rather than simply list names and credentials.

### Geography

Include city, state, and service area naturally when applicable. Include neighborhoods and surrounding markets when they help explain location or service coverage. Do not force geographic keywords or imply a physical location unsupported by practice evidence.

### Medical Claims

Support each medical claim with either a link to a reputable independent medical source or evidence from the practice’s website. Use independent medical sources for general treatment facts and the practice’s website for claims about its own services and care.

Check claims from both sources before using them. Remove guarantees, misleading promises, unsupported statistics, and claims that treatment is risk-free. If the evidence leaves a claim doubtful, omit it. Use qualifications only when they accurately reflect the evidence.

Answer general treatment questions directly. Refer the reader to a clinician for individual suitability and treatment planning. Include safety advice when relevant to the article’s question; do not add unrelated warnings or repeatedly substitute “ask your clinician” for an available answer.
requirements.architecture:
# Architecture

Architecture owns the production flow and component responsibilities that achieve [Product’s required outcomes](product.md#purpose-and-scope). It defines how research, drafting, the single evaluation and revision flow, and article delivery work together, including how missing inputs are handled.

[Writing Standards](writing-standards.md) owns what articles must satisfy. [User Design](userdesign.md) owns the operator and customer experience, including presentation and acceptance interactions. [Data Model](data-model.md) owns records and their meanings; [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) owns implementation discipline and verification methods and evidence. [Release](release.md) owns product deployment and recovery. [AGENTS](../AGENTS.md) owns agent responsibilities and governing-document changes.

## Article Production Flow

Use the assignment to guide topic research, then develop the relevant practice context. Combine the findings and handle gaps under [Research and Resolve](#research-and-resolve) before outlining and drafting. Run the single evaluation and revision flow in [Evaluate and Revise](#evaluate-and-revise) before direct customer delivery under [User Design](userdesign.md#assignment-delivery-and-tracking). Writing Standards owns what the article must satisfy; Engineering owns verification methods and evidence.

Use the assignment brief, research notes, and outline as working context and adjust them as useful. Retain the resulting article and one compact support-and-check record under [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status). [Article Research Material](data-model.md#article-research-material) defines the evidence needed to support the resulting article.

Later findings may change the working interpretation or require a return to topic or practice research. Production adjustments do not require separate compliance reviews at each stage.

### Understand the Assignment

Produce a structured working brief that gives research and writing a clear target.

Use the supplied client, prompt number, original title, SEO/AEO label, reference URLs, and special instructions in the working brief. Keep the supplied assignment distinct from its interpretation. Reference the original assignment in the support-and-check record rather than copy it into a separate permanent brief. Preserve the prompt number through revisions under [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status).

Infer an initial target reader and main question or decision from the supplied assignment. Choose one working interpretation, state it in the brief as a hypothesis with supporting evidence, and use it to guide research. Refine the interpretation and target reader as topic and practice evidence develops; do not maintain competing interpretations.

Identify claims implied by the title that need investigation, including superiority, permanence, pricing, availability, and clinician expertise. The title does not establish their truth. Keep missing inputs explicit when they affect the article's answer or an applicable requirement. The brief must establish the audience, purpose, and supplied constraints without silently replacing the assigned topic; resolve a proposed topic change with Alex.

### Research the Assigned Topic

Use the assignment brief to plan and carry out an article-specific investigation of the questions the article must answer and the claims it needs to support. The plan is working guidance and may change as research develops.

Choose research questions and sources that fit the assignment. Topic research may concern treatments, clinician expertise, a practice's approach, professional training, or an alleged advantage. It is not limited to general medical education. Use practice sources during topic research when the assigned question concerns the practice or a named clinician; the research sequence stays the same.

Use supplied reference URLs as starting points rather than material to rewrite or the only sources to consult. Consult authoritative third-party sources for general treatment facts and practice sources for the practice's own services and care under [Writing Standards' Medical Claims](writing-standards.md#medical-claims). Investigate the claims rather than assume that a reference or the assignment title establishes them.

Include a review of leading organic Google results for the same topic. Derive queries from the assignment and working interpretation, including geography when relevant. Examine reader questions, comparisons, considerations, answer structure, omissions, and weak explanations to inform a more useful original article. Search ranking does not establish medical accuracy, and competitor research does not permit competitor links in the delivered article under [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md#links).

Develop supported answers, practical expectations, and relevant distinctions for the assigned reader. Identify the practice questions needed to develop those answers, and use them to guide [Understand the Practice](#understand-the-practice). Keep supporting evidence and material limits under [Data Model](data-model.md#article-research-material). Findings remain open to revision as practice research develops. Identify questions that only Alex can resolve under [User Design](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback).

### Understand the Practice

Use the assignment brief and topic findings to establish the practice context that helps answer the reader's question. Focus the website review on relevant services, treatments, technology, clinicians, credentials, locations, practice approach, terminology, and differentiators under [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md#content-types). Develop useful practice context before outlining.

Use the site's navigation and sitemap, when available, to discover likely pages for each main treatment or service in the assignment. Read relevant pages and follow links to more specific or complementary information. Search the site for important practice questions that remain unanswered. Combine relevant facts across pages; a service page, product page, clinician biography, gallery, or policy page may each supply different parts of the answer. Build on practice evidence already found during topic research.

Examine relevant text and images, including captions and text within images, using Writing Standards' material categories to guide the search. Find useful service, clinician, educational, contact, and booking links, and investigate relevant practice claims from the brief and topic findings.

Stop expanding the website review when the needed practice questions have supported answers and additional relevant pages mostly repeat information, or when targeted searches yield no further usable evidence. Carry remaining gaps and conflicting facts into [Research and Resolve](#research-and-resolve) before relying on them in the article. Later research or drafting may identify a specific question that requires another website visit.

Keep source evidence and limits needed to use the findings accurately under [Data Model](data-model.md#article-research-material). Preserve correct clinician associations and distinguish physical locations from article target geography and treatments from bookable appointments under [Client Information](data-model.md#client-information). A website image does not establish who or what it depicts; product-brand evidence does not establish every formulation or model.

Use the supported material available. This stage does not require material from every category or a general client model.

### Research and Resolve

Combine topic findings and practice context to establish a supported central answer. Confirm or revise the target reader and working interpretation using the combined evidence, and investigate conflicting information before outlining. Keep the evidence needed to support the article under [Data Model](data-model.md#article-research-material).

A missing fact is required when the article needs it to satisfy [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md), an applicable assignment requirement, or its central answer. Use supported wording or omit the detail when that satisfies the requirements without weakening the answer. Material that could improve an otherwise complete, compliant article is optional.

Handle the remaining gap according to its effect on this article:

- **Optional material:** Prepare the article without it and use [User Design's optional-material comments](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback).
- **A required answer that could change the direction:** Resolve it before drafting when it could change the premise, treatment focus, central answer, or recommendation. Investigate further or bring the specific question to Alex when only he can resolve it. Keep the dependency explicit; a marker does not establish a supported direction.
- **A required fact that can be inserted later:** When Alex can supply the fact without changing the supported direction, draft the supported content and use [User Design's Needs Information process](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback). Apply [Evaluate and Revise](#evaluate-and-revise) before delivery; missing information does not excuse other failures.

Base these decisions on the article's actual needs. Use the supported central answer, practice context, and explicit remaining dependencies to guide [Build the Outline](#build-the-outline).

### Build the Outline

Build the outline from the combined research findings and supported central answer. Arrange reader questions into a useful sequence and plan headings with substantive answers under [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md#section-focus). Integrate supported practice material where it develops those answers. Do not assign section word budgets.

Plan clinician selection under [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md#clinician-selection), useful internal links, appropriate external links, and the closing call to action. Place useful practice material and images where they support an explanation, and identify locations for unresolved required facts and comments.

Adjust coverage or return to the relevant topic or practice research when the outline lacks a supported answer. Combine repetitive sections and omit material that does not support its heading. If research cannot support the assigned answer, bring the specific gap to the operator rather than invent material or silently change the topic. The outline guides drafting; customization is checked in [Evaluate and Revise](#evaluate-and-revise).

### Write the First Draft

Produce a complete article from the outline and supported research under [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md). Adjust the outline and material choices when that improves the article.

Use relevant supported practice material, links, and a customized call to action. Acquire and embed images used in the article with supported captions under [User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards). If an image or other optional material cannot be used, choose another supported approach and keep the evidence needed for the resulting article.

Prepare markers and Google Doc comments for unresolved required facts and applicable optional-material requests under [User Design](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback). Preserve source support for factual claims, including claims introduced during writing and in captions.

Pass the completed article and supporting evidence to Evaluate and Revise. Drafting does not have its own compliance gate or checklist.

### Evaluate and Revise

Check the complete article against every applicable requirement in [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md), its assignment-specific instructions, and the presentation requirements in [User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards). This is the single evaluation and revision flow before delivery. Run it as part of production without a manual trigger or Vikas's article-by-article approval.

Use [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) to perform mechanical checks and editorial and evidence assessment on the resulting text, images, and captions. Assess article quality before measuring the final body-word count under Writing Standards. Evaluate the resulting article. Do not add checks or delivery dependencies for unresolved customer questions.

Identify each failed requirement, its location, and the correction needed. For length failures, remove repetition and lower-value material or develop useful explanations and practice context, returning to research when needed. Preserve necessary information and medical qualifications; do not pad the article or cut essential answers to meet the range.

For the current method in Codex, make a focused correction pass that addresses the findings, including further research or outline changes when needed. Then recheck the resulting article against the full applicable checklist and retain its current assessment under [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status). A separate automated repair engine or open-ended retry loop is not required. If failures remain after the correction pass, report them to the operator and keep the article incomplete pending further work. Do not mark the article ready on the basis of checks against an earlier version.

Handle required facts awaiting Alex's input through User Design's markers, comments, and Needs Information process. The checklist must distinguish these facts from passed requirements, other failures, optional requests, and requirements that do not apply. Missing information does not excuse other failures.

Proceed to delivery only when no failures remain, apart from required facts permitted through the Needs Information process. With required facts resolved, the article may be delivered as Ready for Review. Verification does not establish customer acceptance.

### Deliver to Alex

Deliver the evaluated article directly through the Google Drive, Docs, and Sheet experience in [User Design](userdesign.md#assignment-delivery-and-tracking), without requiring Vikas's approval of the individual article.

Preserve the evaluated text, headings, links, images, captions, and markers in the assigned Google Doc. Embed images inline between paragraphs, place each caption immediately below its image, and add the source-link comment anchored to the caption under [User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards). Deliver the images within the Doc without uploading separate original-image files to Drive. Add missing-information comments under [Review, Revision, and Writing Feedback](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback); plain-text notes do not replace Google Doc comments.

Verify that the actual customer Doc preserves the evaluated article and its required comments under [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification). A local export or successful upload alone does not establish delivery. Correct transfer or rendering failures. If correction changes the evaluated article, use Evaluate and Revise to check the resulting version before claiming delivery complete.

Record the correct Doc link and status in the batch Sheet under [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status). Use Needs Information for required facts awaiting Alex; otherwise use Ready for Review after the checks pass. Delivery is complete when the Doc, comments, link, and status are correct.

When Alex provides information or feedback, revise the same Doc and use Evaluate and Revise before updating its status under User Design. Accepted requires Alex's confirmation.
requirements.engineering:
# Engineering

Engineering owns implementation discipline and verification. It defines how product changes are developed, investigated, and reviewed, and which methods and evidence establish that articles and product behavior satisfy their requirements.

[Product](product.md) owns the required outcomes and scope; [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md) owns article requirements; [User Design](userdesign.md) owns the operator and customer experience. [Architecture](architecture.md#evaluate-and-revise) owns the single article evaluation and revision flow; Engineering defines how to verify its requirements without adding editorial obligations or another revision flow. [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status) owns assessment records. [Release](release.md) owns product deployment and recovery; [AGENTS](../AGENTS.md) owns agent responsibilities and governing-document changes.

## Article Verification

Establish whether the resulting article meets [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md), applicable assignment-specific instructions, and [User Design's presentation requirements](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards). Those documents own the requirements; verification does not add editorial obligations. [Architecture](architecture.md#evaluate-and-revise) owns when checking and revision occur.

Use a checklist covering every applicable requirement, with its conditions and exceptions intact. Articles must be fact checked, edited, and substantially verified before delivery; never deliver AI-generated content without substantial editing and verification. AI may assist research, brainstorming, outlining, drafting, and phone checks. Mechanical checks may establish counts, formatting, and other directly measurable properties. Editorial assessment must establish reader usefulness, heading relevance, distinct coverage, voice, and meaningful practice customization under Writing Standards. Evidence assessment must establish factual support, correct associations, and justified medical qualifications. Complete grammar and spelling checks and a final proofread against Writing Standards, including its voice, reader fit, and writing conventions. A passed count or supported claim alone does not establish editorial quality.

Verify [Clinician Selection](writing-standards.md#clinician-selection) by counting the clinicians featured against the stated limit and checking the evidence for their experience, expertise, treatment involvement, and attributed approach. Assess whether the article gives the reader a supported reason to consider each clinician for the concern discussed.

Verify [Readability](writing-standards.md#readability) by counting prose body paragraphs and the sentences in each. Exclude headings, list items, captions, and comments; account for abbreviations and initials when identifying sentence boundaries. Record the number and proportion of body paragraphs containing one or two sentences in the final assessment. Review whether parallel information would be clearer as bullets, and identify passages that need that change.

Verify [Reader Priorities](writing-standards.md#reader-priorities), [Article Voice](writing-standards.md#article-voice), and [Section Focus](writing-standards.md#section-focus) by reading the completed article section by section and across sections. Establish the question or subject stated by each heading, then check whether each paragraph, bullet, and example develops that answer through facts, explanations, comparisons, examples, or necessary qualifications. Identify useful passages that belong under another heading and sections that overlap without adding distinct value. For first-time treatment articles, check whether the relevant sequence is understandable and whether the evidence supports any stated practice process or visit timing. Assess whether important facts are connected to their supported practical meaning and whether the language sounds natural. Identify passages that give advice instead of an available answer, repeat a point without developing it, or add generic warnings after the relevant limitation is already clear. Stock-phrase searches and paragraph counts cannot establish these results.

Support each checklist result with evidence appropriate to the requirement. For editorial results, point to representative passages in the exact article and explain how they satisfy the writing requirement. A list of present facts, links, qualifications, or clinician names is not enough to establish reader usefulness. Record concrete violations as failures with their locations and needed corrections; do not mark the requirement passed while leaving those violations as editorial caveats. Retain concise evidence in the final-check portion of the support-and-check record under [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status).

Use source evidence to establish factual claims and included images or captions. For the practice-substitution test under [Customization](writing-standards.md#customization), identify actual content or images that need substantive rewriting or replacement for another practice offering the same services. Distinguish that evidence from the article's general educational value; passing substitution alone does not establish useful explanations.

Verify each caption under [Images](writing-standards.md#images): check whether it explains a supported point the image illustrates, connects to the nearby content, and includes limits needed for accurate interpretation. Inspect the rendered article to establish image legibility, placement, proportions, caption presentation, and preservation of meaning under [User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards). Planned use or a source URL does not prove that an image is present. Do not report an unavailable input or an unperformed check as a pass.

Use [Data Model's assessment distinctions](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status) for passes, failures, required facts awaiting Alex, optional requests, and requirements that do not apply. An absent optional feature does not itself establish failure. Measure body words using Writing Standards' range and counting scope, and record the count in the assessment rather than the customer article.

Verify the exact resulting article version identified in the support-and-check record. Findings guide [Architecture's single evaluation and revision flow](architecture.md#evaluate-and-revise). Update the record with the final recheck outcome rather than retain separate correction reports. [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status) defines its contents and retention limits.

Before claiming delivery complete, verify that the actual customer Doc preserves the evaluated article and required comments under [Architecture](architecture.md#deliver-to-alex). Confirm that each image is embedded inline, its caption appears immediately below it, and the caption's Google Doc comment contains the correct source links under [User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards). Inspect the delivered image's legibility and proportions. Local checks establish only the local result. If delivery changes content or presentation, assess the resulting version through Architecture's evaluation flow.

Keep local image files only while needed to create or verify the article. Remove those files when that need ends; a separate original-image archive is not required for delivery or proof of completion. Keep the source references and supporting context under [Data Model](data-model.md#article-research-material).

Verification supports direct delivery without Vikas's article-by-article approval. It does not establish customer acceptance or assessment reliability across assignments. [User Design](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback) defines Alex's review and acceptance.
requirements.data-model:
# Data Model

Data Model owns records and their meanings, identity, relationships, and validity. It defines how assignments, practice information, source evidence, article assessments, and statuses are represented.

[Product](product.md) owns the required outcomes and scope; [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md) owns article requirements. [Architecture](architecture.md#article-production-flow) owns how production creates and uses these records. [User Design](userdesign.md) owns how information is presented to Vikas and Alex; [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) owns the verification evidence recorded in assessments. [Release](release.md) owns compatibility and recovery for deployed data changes. [AGENTS](../AGENTS.md) owns agent responsibilities and governing-document changes.

## Client Information

Client information must accommodate multiple websites and physical locations. It must distinguish physical locations from article target geography, and treatments from bookable appointments. Clinician roles, credentials, and treatment associations must refer to the correct person.

[User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards) defines how articles reflect client information and make missing or conflicting information visible.

## Article Research Material

Keep source links and the passages needed to verify the resulting article's factual claims, practice associations, images, and captions in its support-and-check record under [Assignments and Article Status](#assignments-and-article-status). Retain material limits or conflicts when they affect those claims or unresolved issues. Sources can support several passages; do not repeat the same evidence for each occurrence. [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md#content-types) owns material eligibility.

Distinguish source statements from interpretation and unknown associations from confirmed ones. A website image does not by itself establish that it depicts the practice or its work; evidence for one product does not establish another formulation or device model. For each included image, keep the source page link, direct image link, and context supporting its use. [User Design](userdesign.md#article-content-and-writing-standards) defines the source-link comment Alex receives; a separate original-image archive is not required.

## Assignments and Article Status

The assignment prompt number remains fixed through revisions. [User Design](userdesign.md#assignment-delivery-and-tracking) defines its presentation in article filenames and the batch Sheet.

Retain two items for each article version: the article, including its used images and customer comments, and one compact support-and-check record. The record contains:

- **Identity:** A reference to the original assignment and the exact article version checked.
- **Production inputs:** The repository commit used for production. If relevant inputs were uncommitted, include their exact diff; the commit alone does not identify those inputs.
- **Claim support:** The source evidence required by [Article Research Material](#article-research-material).
- **Final checks:** The outcome for every applicable requirement, concise evidence sufficient to establish each result, and the measured body-word count. A failure identifies the requirement, location, and correction needed. Keep required facts awaiting Alex, optional requests, and inapplicable requirements distinct from passes and other failures. Identify unperformed or unverified checks explicitly.
- **Unresolved issues:** Only issues that still affect verification, revision, or delivery. While comments have not been posted to the article Doc, keep their text and anchors here so they can be transferred accurately.

The article assessment is the final-check portion of this record. [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) owns how evidence establishes each result; [Architecture](architecture.md#evaluate-and-revise) owns checking and revision.

Briefs, plans, outlines, investigation notes, intermediate checks, and transfer files are working material. They do not require separate retention after the article and support-and-check record contain the needed evidence and unresolved issues. Do not retain production histories or duplicate research, assessment, and provenance records. Preserve reviewed article versions; replacing working material does not authorize deleting those versions.

Article status has the following meanings, using the labels defined in [User Design](userdesign.md#assignment-delivery-and-tracking):

- Drafting: The article is being prepared for Alex's review; this includes unresolved checklist failures before delivery.
- Needs Information: A draft is available with required facts still missing and no other unresolved checklist failures.
- Ready for Review: Required facts are resolved and the resulting article has passed the applicable checks for Alex's editorial review.
- Revising: Alex's information or editorial feedback is being incorporated.
- Accepted: Alex has confirmed that the completed article meets his expectations, with no unresolved required facts.

[User Design](userdesign.md#review-revision-and-writing-feedback) defines the customer review interactions and status changes.
requirements.userdesign:
# User Design

User Design owns the operator and customer experience: what Vikas can accomplish and inspect, how articles are presented and delivered to Alex, and how Alex provides information, feedback, and acceptance. It defines product interactions, presentation, and interface language. [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md) owns the articles’ content and writing voice.

[Product](product.md) owns the required outcomes and scope. [Architecture](architecture.md#article-production-flow) owns how production fulfills this experience; [Data Model](data-model.md) owns records and their meanings; [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) owns verification. [Release](release.md) owns product deployment and recovery. [AGENTS](../AGENTS.md) owns agent conduct, communication with the operator, and governing-document changes.

## Article Content and Writing Standards

Articles must meet [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md), the consolidated content and writing specification. That document owns the style-guide baseline, assignment additions, applicability, approved interpretations, material eligibility, and writing conventions.

Present images and captions that meet [Writing Standards](writing-standards.md#images) in the same Google Doc as the article. Embed each image inline between paragraphs and place its caption immediately below it. Add a Google Doc comment anchored to the caption containing the source page link and the direct image link when it differs from the page link.

Images and relevant labels must be clear enough to read, with proportions preserved and without cropping that changes their meaning. An image link or placement note does not replace an embedded image. Delivery does not include separate original-image files in Drive.

Vikas receives the compact support-and-check record for the resulting article, including its final checklist outcome, remaining failures, and required facts awaiting Alex. This supports confidence in delivery without requiring Vikas to approve each article. [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status) defines the record and status meanings.

The system delivers articles directly to Alex under [Assignment Delivery and Tracking](#assignment-delivery-and-tracking). Missing required facts and optional material follow [Review, Revision, and Writing Feedback](#review-revision-and-writing-feedback). [Data Model](data-model.md#article-research-material) defines retained research evidence, and [Client Information](data-model.md#client-information) defines valid client associations. [Architecture](architecture.md#article-production-flow) owns production and the single evaluation and revision flow; [Engineering](engineering.md#article-verification) owns verification methods and evidence.

## Assignment Delivery and Tracking

The system prepares and delivers assigned articles directly to Alex without requiring Vikas to review or approve individual articles. Vikas can monitor assignment progress, delivered articles, and unresolved issues through the batch Sheet and article Docs.

Each assignment batch has a Google Drive folder containing one subfolder per client and one Google Doc per article.

Each Doc’s filename includes the client name, assignment prompt number, SEO or AEO type, and article title so Alex can match the article to its assignment. [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status) defines the fixed prompt number through revisions.

The batch folder contains a Google Sheet with one row per assigned article. Each row includes the client, prompt number, SEO or AEO type, article title, Doc link, and status. The initial batch tracks all 52 articles in [Product’s assignment scope](product.md#assignment-scope).

The supported status labels are Drafting, Needs Information, Ready for Review, Revising, and Accepted. [Data Model](data-model.md#assignments-and-article-status) defines their meanings. The [Review, Revision, and Writing Feedback](#review-revision-and-writing-feedback) section defines the review interactions and status changes.

## Review, Revision, and Writing Feedback

Delivered articles must meet the applicable company, client, and assignment requirements and match the quality of content produced by Benchmark’s writers. Alex reviews the articles as the customer. In the current product version, this provides human review after delivery; human review is not required before delivery. AI review does not establish human review or acceptance. Customer confirmation remains open in [Roadmap](roadmap.md#open-questions-for-alex). Acceptance depends on both compliance with the writing standards and Alex’s subjective judgment of the article’s content and quality. Alex’s acceptance determines whether the articles meet [Product’s quality goal](product.md#purpose-and-scope).

Alex reviews each article through comments and suggested edits in its Google Doc. Revisions use the same Doc and address his feedback. The batch Sheet records the article’s current status.

Alex is the contact for missing or conflicting client information. [Architecture's Research and Resolve](architecture.md#research-and-resolve) determines whether to omit a detail, resolve the article's direction before drafting, or deliver supported content with a required fact awaiting Alex. Use the following comments and status interactions for gaps that can remain in the delivered article.

For missing optional material, prepare the article without that material and add a comment at the relevant location explaining what could improve the article and asking Alex to supply it. Optional requests do not prevent Ready for Review.

For a required fact that can be inserted without changing the supported direction, place a clear marker where the fact belongs and add a Google Doc comment explaining what Alex must supply or confirm. Deliver as Needs Information only after the article passes the applicable checks apart from the permitted missing facts, under [Architecture](architecture.md#evaluate-and-revise). Alex can answer in the comment or suggest text directly.

When Alex supplies the required information, move the article to Revising while incorporating it. Once required facts are resolved and the revised article passes [Architecture's evaluation and revision flow](architecture.md#evaluate-and-revise), move the article to Ready for Review.

Completing revisions does not itself establish acceptance. Alex confirms acceptance; unresolved required facts prevent Accepted status.

Alex’s feedback guides revisions to the current article and, where applicable, improvements to future writing for that client or across clients.

cases.assignment: Explain what a first vascular-laser visit and recovery involve at fictional Harbor Clinic.
cases.heading: Recovery After Treatment

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Harbor offers vascular laser treatment for visible facial vessels. Its published aftercare states that mild redness may last two to three days, cold compresses may ease discomfort, and strenuous exercise should be avoided for 24 hours. An independent educational source confirms these general recovery expectations and says persistent or worsening symptoms should be reported to the treating team. No special social-media issue or additional checklist risk is documented.

cases.section:
Mild redness can remain for two to three days after treatment. Harbor recommends a cold compress for discomfort and a 24-hour pause from strenuous exercise, so leave that activity out of your schedule on treatment day.

Contact the treating team if symptoms persist or worsen. That is different from judging the appearance during the first few hours, when ordinary redness may still be present.

These measures support a considered recovery process, but no checklist can cover every personal circumstance. Keeping the wider picture in mind allows the treatment and your individual needs to remain part of the same conversation.

cases.assignment: Explain clinician roles for a first radiofrequency microneedling visit at fictional Summit Clinic.
cases.heading: Who Performs the Procedure?

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Summit lists Dr. Elena Reed, a board-certified dermatologist, as consultation lead, and nurse practitioner Omar Chen as a clinician trained in radiofrequency microneedling. It does not identify who performs each booked procedure or the supervision arrangement. Independent general evidence supports discussing treatment goals, skin conditions and prior reactions at assessment. No claim about specific operator assignment can be made from the profiles.

cases.section:
Dr. Elena Reed leads Summit’s consultations and is a board-certified dermatologist. Her skin-health background is relevant when texture concerns occur alongside an existing skin condition.

Omar Chen is a nurse practitioner trained in radiofrequency microneedling. His treatment training gives another supported reason to consider him for this procedure.

The profiles establish relevant experience, but they do not identify the clinician assigned to your appointment. Confirm who will perform the procedure and what supervision is provided when booking.

cases.assignment: Explain the treatment assessment for fictional Cedar Clinic radiofrequency microneedling.
cases.heading: How Settings Are Chosen

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Cedar confirms an adjustable-depth radiofrequency microneedling device and an assessment of treatment area, skin thickness, texture concern and previous reactions. An independent educational source explains that needle depth and energy settings are chosen for the area and skin characteristics rather than always using the greatest available depth. Neither source claims that a device model establishes an individual plan.

cases.section:
Cedar’s device allows the clinician to adjust needle depth and energy settings. The published assessment considers the area being treated, skin thickness, the texture concern and previous reactions.

The clinician chooses settings for those characteristics rather than automatically using the greatest available depth. This matters when comparing treatment of areas with different skin thickness.

The device specifications belong within a broader review rather than standing in for it. Keeping the assessment in its proper place helps the technology remain relevant to the person receiving treatment.

cases.assignment: Explain a fictional Oak Clinic booking policy relevant to a first chemical-peel visit.
cases.heading: Changing Your Appointment

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Oak requires a booking deposit. Its written policy states that rescheduling less than 48 hours before an appointment may mean the deposit is retained and a new deposit is required for another booking. The article need not reproduce every policy detail; a supported statement that a late schedule change can affect the deposit is accurate. No conflicting policy exists in this scenario.

cases.section:
Oak takes a deposit when you book a chemical-peel appointment. A late change to your appointment can affect that deposit, so check the rescheduling terms before confirming a date you may need to move.

Keep the booking confirmation available if you need to contact the practice about a change.

cases.assignment: Explain a fictional Linden Clinic comparison of intense pulsed light and fractional resurfacing.
cases.heading: Choosing Between Light Treatment and Resurfacing

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Linden offers both treatments. The independent source explains that intense pulsed light can address pigment spots and visible vessels, whereas fractional resurfacing creates small treatment zones to address texture and fine lines. Choice depends on the concern and skin assessment. Both may be considered for separate concerns, but no specific combined-treatment protocol is documented. These general facts and service associations are confirmed within this scenario.

cases.section:
Intense pulsed light uses light energy to target pigment spots and visible vessels. Fractional resurfacing creates small treatment zones in the skin to address texture and fine lines.

Linden offers both services. Their different targets make the feature you want to change the useful starting point, rather than choosing whichever treatment sounds more powerful.

Either treatment, or a combination when suitable, should fit the concern under discussion. The availability of two approaches does not make either one automatic, and a considered plan keeps both options in perspective.

cases.assignment: Explain a fictional clinician-training course without inventing professional eligibility.
cases.heading: What the Course Certificate Means

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: The Meridian course is for licensed clinicians. It provides a certificate of attendance for completion of a day of facial-anatomy teaching and demonstration. The course does not award board certification or an additional professional license. Participants remain subject to their existing professional scope and local rules. No specific jurisdiction is named; no legal eligibility determination is required in this diagnostic.

cases.section:
Meridian’s course combines facial-anatomy teaching with treatment demonstrations for licensed clinicians. The certificate records attendance at that day of training.

It does not award board certification or a new professional license. Those are different credentials, so describe the course as training when discussing your qualifications rather than presenting its certificate as specialist certification.

cases.assignment: Explain the first chemical-peel visit at fictional Willow Clinic.
cases.heading: What Happens at the Consultation?

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Willow publishes a consultation route but not a detailed consultation checklist. An independent medical source describes a general peel assessment that considers skin condition, treatment goals, current medicines and a history of reactions. It does not establish Willow’s own checklist, clinician process, peel concentration or medication-stopping instructions. The scenario is complete; no unpublished Willow protocol can be assumed.

cases.section:
Willow’s consultation includes a review of your treatment goals, skin condition, medicines and past reactions. Its clinician uses that review to choose a peel concentration before discussing the likely recovery.

Bring your medication list rather than deciding on your own which prescriptions to stop. The appointment gives you a chance to describe the change you want to see.

cases.assignment: Explain a fictional Meadow Clinic treatment with a supported delayed result.
cases.heading: When the Result Becomes Visible

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Meadow confirms a treatment for uneven pigment whose changes develop over several weeks. Its source gives an initial review at four weeks and distinguishes temporary redness in the first two days from later pigment improvement. The independent source corroborates that visible treatment change is delayed. Timing varies. No event-readiness or guaranteed cosmetic outcome is established.

cases.section:
The pigment change develops over several weeks rather than appearing fully on treatment day. Meadow schedules an initial review at four weeks, when the clinician can assess the developing result.

Redness during the first two days is a separate recovery effect. An early photograph may record that redness rather than the improvement you are waiting to see, so it is not a fair comparison with the four-week review.

cases.assignment: Explain the commitment involved in a fictional Brook Clinic treatment course.
cases.heading: Why Appointments Are Spaced Apart

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Brook publishes a typical treatment course with appointments spaced four to six weeks apart. The independent educational source explains that skin recovery and later assessment require time between visits, and that improvement develops across the course. Timing is individually set. No fixed completion date or guaranteed number of visits is supported.

cases.section:
Brook commonly spaces appointments four to six weeks apart. That interval gives the skin time to recover and allows the clinician to assess the developing change before the next visit.

The appointments are separated because recovery and assessment take time. Space between treatments supports the ongoing course, rather than treating each visit as if it were separate from the visits around it.

Allow calendar time for the gaps as well as the appointments. The clinician sets the schedule for your course; the published interval is a planning guide, not a fixed completion date.

cases.assignment: Explain a fictional Vale Clinic comfort option and its limits.
cases.heading: Comfort During Treatment

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Vale uses cooling during a light-based treatment. Independent medical evidence confirms cooling can reduce discomfort but cannot guarantee absence of pain or burns. Device settings and skin characteristics affect risk. Cooling does not eliminate the need for appropriate settings. This section is the first mention of these particular limits; they have not already been stated elsewhere in the supplied context. The independent source explicitly describes a snapping or warm sensation during light pulses.

cases.section:
Vale uses cooling while the light pulses are delivered. Cooling can reduce discomfort, but a snapping or warm sensation may still occur.

It also does not make burns impossible. Appropriate settings still matter because the skin absorbs some of the delivered energy; cooling is a comfort measure, not proof that every setting is safe for your skin.

cases.assignment: Explain a fictional Ash Clinic comparison with original prose.
cases.heading: Choosing the Feature to Change

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Independent medical source: treatment A addresses visible pigment spots; treatment B addresses surface texture and fine lines. Ash confirms offering both. Synthetic competitor expression: “Picture your skin as a photograph: light treatment erases stray ink from the image, while resurfacing changes the grain of the paper beneath it.” That photograph/ink/paper analogy is distinctive competitor expression, not required medical terminology. No source requires this analogy.

cases.section:
Think of your skin as a printed photograph: light treatment removes unwanted ink from the picture, while resurfacing alters the grain of the paper underneath. These are different changes, so Ash offers both approaches for different concerns.

A pigment spot and a rough patch can look noticeable for different reasons. Describe which feature bothers you rather than assuming that one treatment must change both.

cases.assignment: Explain a fictional Pine Clinic assessment without filling an evidence gap.
cases.heading: What the First Appointment Establishes

evidence.type: Complete hypothetical source context for this diagnostic; not real clinical advice.
evidence.text: Pine confirms a consultation that reviews aesthetic goals and medical history before a tailored plan. Its booking page does not say that a procedure occurs at the consultation appointment. Independent evidence supports individual suitability assessment. The article concerns a first visit, so whether consultation includes treatment is a relevant timing uncertainty. No other limitation or follow-up process is needed here.

cases.section:
Pine starts with a consultation about your aesthetic goals and medical history, then develops a tailored plan.

The booking page does not confirm that treatment happens during that appointment. If you are reserving time away from work for a procedure, confirm whether you are booking assessment alone or assessment and treatment.

shared_limits: Read only this packet. Do not read repository files, prior reviews, protocols, answer keys, other tasks, or result files. Do not browse live sources.
Each case is a standalone section excerpt with its entire relevant scenario evidence. These hypothetical facts define the diagnostic world; they are not real medical recommendations.
Judge each case independently; cases are not pairs, and there is no prescribed number of passing or failing cases. Do not infer a label distribution.

Apply only requirements relevant to the excerpt. Do not require full-article length, CTA, four links, two clinicians, images, or every stage of care in an isolated section. Assess prose and claims actually present.
Mark unsupported assertions unverified or failure as appropriate; never infer a practice protocol from general medical education. Do not substitute external clinical knowledge for the given evidence.
For every failure identify an exact passage, existing requirement, reader consequence, evidence, and specific correction. Keep optional improvements and necessary source limits distinct.
Preferences for more detail do not by themselves establish failure. Do not use an AI-authorship score. Agent agreement and persuasive explanations are not proof of correctness.

cases.reader_takeaway: what this section actually helps the assigned reader understand

findings.evidence: supplied source or stated evidence gap

positive_evidence: exact passage and explanation of compliance

common_packet.review_instructions: Apply the frozen Engineering Article Verification procedure and all applicable governing requirements.

overrides.review_instructions:
Apply the unchanged governing standards using reader usefulness, factual credibility, original synthesis and natural voice. Read each section exactly as written before deciding whether it passes. Establish the question its heading promises to answer and the supported answer the reader actually receives. Then examine every paragraph, including section endings, for its actual contribution: new information, supported practical meaning, a relevant distinction, or a necessary qualification. A section with useful facts can still fail because another passage is redundant or abstract.

For a qualification, identify the particular claim or misunderstanding it limits, or the specific unknown it helps the reader resolve. Accuracy and caution alone do not establish usefulness. Generic reminders about individual circumstances, keeping a broad perspective, or the importance of assessment need a concrete contribution under Article Voice and Section Focus. Do not mentally supply an explanation missing from the words. If a passage could become useful after a rewrite, judge the existing passage and describe that rewrite as its correction. Preserve supported safety information and qualifications that prevent a concrete misunderstanding; do not reject all caution or all repetition automatically.

Distinguish required correction from optional improvement. Useful facts need not each contain an action or a practical consequence. A supported concise policy description can be acceptable even when a more specific alternative exists. Different sentence order, greater detail, stronger style preference, or absence of optional material is not by itself a failure. Do not invent a new requirement or lower the existing standard.

Check factual support and association separately from style. General educational evidence does not establish a named practice’s care process. Shared facts do not establish plagiarism, but distinctive borrowed expression can. Every failure needs the exact passage, governing requirement, reader consequence, source support or limit, and correction. Keep unexplained or unsupported claims separate from mere preference. Findings must justify the verdict, not decorate it.

Use the attached operator-calibrated examples to understand the correction threshold; the new diagnostic cases were not used for that calibration. These examples express Vikas’s judgments, not Alex’s acceptance, and do not change current governing requirements.

operator_calibration_examples.purpose: Retain operator judgments needed to compare evaluator findings and calibrate the threshold for required editorial correction. These judgments do not change governing requirements or establish Alex's acceptance.

overrides.review_instructions:
Apply the unchanged governing standards using reader usefulness, factual credibility, original synthesis and natural voice. Read each section exactly as written before deciding whether it passes. Establish the question its heading promises to answer and the supported answer the reader actually receives. Then examine every paragraph, including section endings, for its actual contribution: new information, supported practical meaning, a relevant distinction, or a necessary qualification. A section with useful facts can still fail because another passage is redundant or abstract.

For a qualification, identify the particular claim or misunderstanding it limits, or the specific unknown it helps the reader resolve. Accuracy and caution alone do not establish usefulness. Generic reminders about individual circumstances, keeping a broad perspective, or the importance of assessment need a concrete contribution under Article Voice and Section Focus. Do not mentally supply an explanation missing from the words. If a passage could become useful after a rewrite, judge the existing passage and describe that rewrite as its correction. Preserve supported safety information and qualifications that prevent a concrete misunderstanding; do not reject all caution or all repetition automatically.

Distinguish required correction from optional improvement. Useful facts need not each contain an action or a practical consequence. A supported concise policy description can be acceptable even when a more specific alternative exists. Different sentence order, greater detail, stronger style preference, or absence of optional material is not by itself a failure. Do not invent a new requirement or lower the existing standard.

Check factual support and association separately from style. General educational evidence does not establish a named practice’s care process. Shared facts do not establish plagiarism, but distinctive borrowed expression can. Every failure needs the exact passage, governing requirement, reader consequence, source support or limit, and correction. Keep unexplained or unsupported claims separate from mere preference. Findings must justify the verdict, not decorate it.

Use the attached operator-calibrated examples to understand the correction threshold; the new diagnostic cases were not used for that calibration. These examples express Vikas’s judgments, not Alex’s acceptance, and do not change current governing requirements.
